Chapter 8: The Power—and Peril—of Apology
There’s a certain quiet strength in being able to say, “I was wrong.” But, let’s be honest—those words can feel almost impossible to say out loud. Why is that? Well, for a lot of us, the fear of losing face or being seen as weak or not up to the job can be overwhelming. And yet, refusing to apologize—refusing to own up to our mistakes—usually ends up causing more trouble than the original error ever did.
Picture this: you’re at work, and your manager makes a call that totally backfires. The team is frustrated, morale drops, and underneath it all, resentment starts to build. And what does the manager do? Instead of owning up, they double down—blaming circumstances, pointing fingers, insisting the plan was fine. The team feels it. They start to pull away. Trust takes a hit, and suddenly the workplace feels tense and unwelcoming.
Now, imagine that same manager taking a different approach. They get the team together, take a deep breath, and say, “I made a mistake. I’m sorry for how it affected you. Let’s figure out how to fix it together.” Instantly, the mood shifts. People feel seen and respected. The group starts coming up with solutions. Sure, the mistake isn’t erased—but now, there’s space for repair and growth.
That’s the real power of an apology. It breaks the cycle of self-justification. It shows you’re willing to be vulnerable—to put honesty ahead of pride. But here’s something to pay attention to: not every apology is created equal. A true apology doesn’t try to minimize what happened, or shift the blame, or make excuses. Instead, it’s about truly taking responsibility, acknowledging the harm, and making things right.
A lot of people worry that saying “I’m sorry” makes them look weak. But the truth? It usually has the exact opposite effect. Apologizing builds trust, deepens our relationships, and opens up space for real growth. Whether it’s with family, friends, coworkers, or even entire countries, the courage to apologize can turn conflict into connection.
Of course, apology is just the beginning. Real change shows up through reflection, learning from what happened, and a genuine commitment to do better next time. Our minds will always want to jump in and justify, to protect our egos. But with some practice, we can notice that urge, and gently set it aside.
